chunks: And from him (Al-Shaykh) from Ibrahim ibn Abi Ishaq from Abdullah ibn Hammad al-Ansari from Aban ibn Uthman from Ya'qub ibn Shu'ayb al-Haddad from al-Abd al-Salih (peace be upon him) who said:

I said to him: A man from us is in a remote land; what should he do with the zakat of his wealth? He said: 'Place it among his brothers and those of his Wilayah.' I said: But if none of them are present there with him? He said: 'Send it to them.' I said: But if he cannot find anyone to carry it to them? He said: 'Give it to one who is not a Naṣīb (one who bears enmity towards the Ahl al-Bayt).' I said: And if they (the Ahl al-Bayt/their followers) are not there? He said: 'There is no [specific requirement] for those other than them, except the stone (i.e., it is valid generally).'

key_terms.أَهْلِ وَلَايَتِهِ: Those of Wilayah (followers/relatives of the Imams)
key_terms.الْحَجَرُ: The stone (idiom for general validity or lack of specific restriction)
key_terms.يَنْصِبُ: Naṣīb (one who bears enmity towards the Ahl al-Bayt)

ai.seo_question: How should a Muslim pay zakat if they are in a remote area without access to the Ahl al-Bayt or their agents?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Tahdhib* details the jurisprudential hierarchy for zakat distribution when the primary recipients (Ahl al-Bayt and their deputies) are inaccessible, reflecting the Shia emphasis on Wilayah in financial obligations. It establishes a clear progression from specific kinship ties to general worthy recipients, culminating in the principle that those outside this spiritual lineage ('non-Naṣīb') are entitled only to the 'stone' of zakat, highlighting the theological distinction between Shia and Sunni recipients. This ruling underscores the practical adaptability of Shia fiqh in remote contexts while maintaining doctrinal purity regarding the recipients' spiritual status.
